title: Waves, Sound & Light
description: Wave properties, transverse vs longitudinal, the electromagnetic spectrum, sound, reflection, refraction, and wave behaviour.

notes.heading: Wave Properties and the Wave Equation
notes.body: All waves transfer energy without transferring matter. Key properties: Amplitude — maximum displacement from rest position (related to energy/intensity). Wavelength (λ) — distance between two consecutive identical points (peak to peak, trough to trough). Frequency (f) — number of complete waves per second, measured in Hertz (Hz). 1 Hz = 1 wave/second. Period (T) — time for one complete wave. T = 1/f. Wave speed: v = fλ (m/s). This equation works for all waves — sound, light, water waves. Example: sound wave with f=440 Hz, λ=0.78 m → v=343 m/s. The speed of a wave depends on the medium, not the frequency. Changing frequency changes wavelength proportionally (v constant in a given medium).

illustration.alt: Labelled transverse wave showing amplitude, wavelength, crest, trough, and the wave equation v equals f lambda.
illustration.caption: Waves transfer energy from one place to another without transferring matter.

notes.heading: Transverse and Longitudinal Waves
notes.body: Transverse: particle oscillation is PERPENDICULAR to wave direction. Examples: light, all EM waves, water ripples, S-waves (earthquakes). Can travel through vacuum (EM waves). Crests and troughs. Longitudinal: particle oscillation is PARALLEL to wave direction. Examples: sound, P-waves (earthquakes). Consists of compressions (high pressure, particles close) and rarefactions (low pressure, particles spread). Requires a medium — cannot travel through a vacuum. Sound speed: air ~343 m/s, water ~1500 m/s, steel ~5000 m/s. Denser media transmit sound faster (particles closer, vibrations pass faster). Ripples on water are mainly transverse; seismic P-waves are longitudinal; S-waves are transverse (S-waves cannot pass through liquid outer core — evidence Earth has a liquid core).

illustration.alt: Side-by-side comparison of transverse waves (light, water) and longitudinal waves (sound).
illustration.caption: In transverse waves, oscillations are perpendicular to energy transfer; in longitudinal waves, they are parallel.

notes.heading: The Electromagnetic Spectrum
notes.body: The EM spectrum is a continuous family of transverse waves all travelling at 3×10⁸ m/s in a vacuum. Ordered by increasing frequency (decreasing wavelength): Radio waves (longest λ, communication, broadcasting), Microwaves (cooking, satellite transmission, WiFi), Infrared (thermal imaging, remote controls, heating), Visible light (detected by human eye, ROYGBIV — red longest λ, violet shortest), Ultraviolet (UV — tanning, sterilisation, fluorescent lamps, causes skin cancer), X-rays (medical imaging, security scanners, can damage DNA), Gamma rays (shortest λ, highest energy, cancer treatment, sterilising medical equipment). Energy increases with frequency: gamma rays are the most energetic and dangerous (ionising — can knock electrons off atoms, damaging DNA). UV, X-ray, and gamma are ionising. Radio, microwave, infrared, and visible are non-ionising. Uses determined by wavelength: long λ = diffraction around obstacles (radio); short λ = high resolution imaging (X-rays).

illustration.alt: Full electromagnetic spectrum from radio waves to gamma rays, showing decreasing wavelength and increasing frequency.
illustration.caption: All electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light in a vacuum and are transverse waves.

notes.heading: Sound Waves
notes.body: Sound is a longitudinal wave produced by vibrating objects. The vibration compresses and rarefies air particles → pressure wave travels outward. Properties: Pitch = frequency (higher f = higher pitch). Human hearing range: ~20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Ultrasound: f > 20 kHz — used for medical imaging (foetal scans), sonar, cleaning. Infrasound: f < 20 Hz — elephants communicate, earthquake detection. Loudness = amplitude (larger amplitude = louder sound, more energy). Sound intensity decreases with distance (energy spreads over larger area). Speed of sound depends on medium: faster in solids (particles tightly coupled), slower in gases. Temperature affects speed: warmer air = faster sound (particles move faster). Echo: sound reflection. Time delay between original sound and echo depends on distance to reflecting surface (v=2d/t). Sonar uses this principle.

illustration.alt: How sound travels as longitudinal compression and rarefaction in air, with properties and the echo method for measuring speed.
illustration.caption: Sound is a longitudinal wave that cannot travel through a vacuum.

notes.heading: Reflection and Refraction
notes.body: Reflection: waves bounce off a surface. Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection (measured from the normal — an imaginary line perpendicular to surface). Specular reflection: smooth surface → parallel rays reflected parallel → clear image (mirror). Diffuse reflection: rough surface → rays scattered in all directions → no clear image (paper, wall). Refraction: waves change direction when crossing a boundary between media of different densities at an angle (due to speed change). Entering denser medium (e.g., air → glass): wave slows down → bends TOWARDS the normal. Entering less dense medium: speeds up → bends AWAY from normal. If entering along the normal (0°): no bending, just speed change. Refraction explains: lenses focusing light, apparent depth (pool looks shallower), mirages (hot air bends light), broken pencil illusion in water.

illustration.alt: Wavefront diagrams showing reflection at a barrier and refraction as waves change speed in different depths of water.
illustration.caption: Refraction occurs when waves change speed at a boundary, causing them to change direction.

notes.heading: Dispersion and Colour
notes.body: White light is a mixture of all visible colours (ROYGBIV). Dispersion: splitting white light into its constituent colours using a prism (refraction). Different colours have different wavelengths → refract by different amounts in glass. Violet refracts most (shortest λ, slowest in glass); red refracts least (longest λ, fastest in glass). Rainbow formation: sunlight refracted and internally reflected in water droplets → dispersed. Colour of objects: a red object reflects red light, absorbs all other colours. A white object reflects all colours. A black object absorbs all colours (heats up most in sunlight). Filters: a red filter transmits only red light, absorbs others. Colour mixing: additive (light) — red+green+blue = white (RGB — screens, stage lighting). Subtractive (pigments/paints) — cyan+magenta+yellow = black (CMY — printing). The primary colours for light are red, green, blue.

illustration.alt: Prism splitting white light into rainbow colours, showing that different frequencies refract by different amounts.
illustration.caption: White light disperses into a spectrum because each colour travels at a slightly different speed in glass.

notes.heading: Wave Behaviour: Diffraction, Absorption, Transmission
notes.body: When waves encounter materials or obstacles: Absorption — wave energy is taken in by material (e.g., black surfaces absorb light → heat up; soundproofing foam absorbs sound energy). Transmission — wave passes through material (e.g., glass transmits visible light; ultrasound transmits through soft tissue, reflects off bone). Diffraction — waves spread out after passing through a gap or around an obstacle. Maximum diffraction when gap size ≈ wavelength. This is why: you can hear sound around corners (sound λ ~ 0.1-10 m, comparable to door width), but light does NOT noticeably diffract around corners (light λ ~ 400-700 nm, very small). Radio waves diffract around hills (long λ) — why radio works even without line-of-sight. Microwaves (shorter λ) require line-of-sight for communication. Wavefront diagrams show diffraction: straight wavefronts hitting a gap → curved wavefronts emerging. This is Huygens' principle.

illustration.alt: Wave behaviour at boundaries: transmission, absorption, and diffraction of waves around edges and through gaps.
illustration.caption: Diffraction is greatest when the gap size is similar to the wavelength of the wave.

flashcards.definition: Number of complete waves per second. Measured in Hertz (Hz). 1 Hz = 1 wave/s.
flashcards.example: 440 Hz = 440 wave cycles every second — the musical note A.

flashcards.definition: Distance between two consecutive peaks or troughs. Measured in metres.
flashcards.example: Visible light: λ ~400 nm (violet) to ~700 nm (red).

flashcards.definition: v = fλ. Wave speed = frequency × wavelength. Applies to ALL waves.
flashcards.example: Sound: f=500 Hz, λ=0.68 m → v=340 m/s.

flashcards.definition: Particle oscillation perpendicular to wave direction. Light, EM waves, water ripples.
flashcards.example: Rope shaken up/down — wave travels horizontally, rope moves vertically.

flashcards.definition: Particle oscillation parallel to wave direction. Sound, P-waves.
flashcards.example: Slinky pushed/pulled along its length — compressions and rarefactions travel along.

flashcards.definition: Increasing f: Radio → Microwave → Infrared → Visible → UV → X-ray → Gamma. All travel at c=3×10⁸ m/s in vacuum.
flashcards.example: Gamma rays have the highest frequency and energy; radio waves the lowest.

flashcards.definition: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection, measured from the normal.
flashcards.example: Light hitting mirror at 30° to normal → reflected at 30° on other side.

flashcards.definition: Wave changes direction crossing boundary between media of different density (speed changes).
flashcards.example: Pencil appears bent in water — light speeds up entering air, bends away from normal.

flashcards.definition: Splitting white light into ROYGBIV colours by refraction (prism). Violet refracts most; red least.
flashcards.example: Rainbow — sunlight dispersed by water droplets. Pink Floyd album cover.

flashcards.definition: Sound with f > 20,000 Hz — above human hearing. Used for medical imaging and sonar.
flashcards.example: Foetal ultrasound scans use 2-18 MHz waves that reflect off tissue boundaries.

flashcards.definition: Waves spread out after passing through a gap. Maximum when gap ≈ wavelength.
flashcards.example: Sound diffracts around doorway (λ ~1 m); light does not (λ ~500 nm) — gap too large.

flashcards.definition: Primary colours of light: Red + Green + Blue = White. Used in screens (RGB pixels).
flashcards.example: Yellow on a screen = red + green pixels lit together.

questions.stem: f=200 Hz, λ=2 m. Wave speed?
questions.explanation: Wave speed is frequency times wavelength: $v=f\lambda=200\times2=400\text{ m/s}$.

questions.stem: Which wave type has particles vibrating at right angles to wave direction?
questions.explanation: Transverse waves oscillate perpendicular to travel direction.

questions.stem: Why can light travel through space but sound cannot?
choices: Sound is mechanical — needs particles; space is a vacuum. Light is EM — no medium needed
questions.explanation: Sound requires particle vibration → no particles in space → no sound. EM waves self-propagate through electric/magnetic fields.
Gamma: shortest λ, highest f, most energetic. Radio: longest λ, lowest f.
Amplitude = energy = loudness. Frequency = pitch. They are independent.

questions.stem: Light hits mirror at 40° to surface. What is angle of incidence?
questions.explanation: Angle of incidence is measured from the NORMAL (perpendicular to surface). 90°−40°=50°.

questions.stem: Why does a pool look shallower than it is?
choices: Refraction — light from the bottom speeds up entering air, bends away from normal → image appears higher
It's an optical illusion with no physical cause
questions.explanation: Light rays from the pool bottom refract at the water-air boundary, bending away from the normal. Brain traces them back in straight lines → shallower apparent depth.

questions.stem: A red filter appears red because:
choices: It transmits only red light, absorbing all other colours
It converts all colours to red
questions.explanation: Filters transmit their own colour and absorb complementary colours. Red filter → red passes; blue, green absorbed.

choices: Steel — denser medium, particles closer → vibrations transmit faster
questions.explanation: Speed: solid > liquid > gas. Particles are closer in solids → vibrations pass more rapidly. Vacuum: zero (no particles).

questions.stem: Why can you hear sound around a corner but not see around it?
choices: Sound λ (~1 m) ≈ door width → strong diffraction. Light λ (~500 nm) << door → negligible diffraction
questions.explanation: Diffraction is significant when gap ≈ wavelength. Sound wavelength matches everyday gaps; light's wavelength is microscopic.

questions.stem: A wave has period 0.02 s. What is its frequency?
questions.explanation: f=1/T=1/0.02=50 Hz. This is UK mains electricity frequency.

questions.stem: Which EM waves are ionising (can damage DNA)?
questions.explanation: UV, X-ray, and gamma have enough photon energy to ionise atoms (knock electrons off) → DNA damage → cancer risk.

questions.stem: A sound wave has f=1000 Hz in air (v=340 m/s). What is λ?
In a prism, red light bends ___ than violet because red has ___ wavelength.
choices: Less; longer — longer λ = less refraction
questions.explanation: Dispersion: longer λ (red) refracts less; shorter λ (violet) refracts more. Red is fastest in glass; violet slowest.

questions.stem: Green + red light projected on a white screen produces:
questions.explanation: Additive (light) mixing: R+G=Yellow, R+B=Magenta, G+B=Cyan, R+G+B=White.
